question_text: In 14th century, during outbreak of Plague, quarantine of ship sailors was done for
explanation:
QUARANTINE

  • Quarantine has been defined as "the limitation of freedom of movement of healthy persons or domestic animals exposed to communicable disease for a period of time not longer than the longest usual incubation period of the disease, in such a manner as to prevent effective contact with those not so exposed".
  • Quarantine measures are also "applied by a health authority to a ship, an aircraft, a train, road vehicle, other means of transport or container, to prevent the spread of disease, reservoirs of disease or vectors of disease".
  • Quarantine was first applied for plague and was done for 40 days.
  • Quarantine means "40 Days".
  • Quarantine can be of :
    • ABSOLUTE QUARANTINE
    • MODIFIED QUARANTINE: Selective partial limitation of freedom of movement, such as exclusion of children from school; and
    • Segregation is defined as "the separation for special consideration, control of observation of some part of a group of persons (or domestic animals) from the others to facilitate control of a communicable disease, e.g., removal of susceptible children to homes of immune persons".

In contrast to isolation, quarantine applies to restrictions on the healthy contacts of an infectious disease.

Quarantine has been 'replaced with active surveillance'

question_text: When quarantine was first implemented in the 14th century to control the plague, for how many days were individuals suspected of infection required to be isolated?
explanation:
Explanation:

The term quarantine comes from the Italian word "quaranta ," which means 40.

During the 14th century, amidst the bubonic plague outbreak, port cities like Venice enforced a regulation requiring ships arriving from infected areas to remain anchored for 40 days before allowing passengers or crew to disembark.

This 40-day isolation period was chosen based on both practical observations and religious beliefs, as it was thought to be sufficient to reveal any signs of illness in those potentially exposed.

Public Health Strategies:

  • Isolation involves separating individuals who are already infected and potentially contagious. This is done for the full duration of communicability and may take place in a healthcare facility or at home, depending on the severity of illness and available resources. It serves as a defensive measure to prevent disease spread.
  • Quarantine refers to the separation and restriction of movement of individuals who have been exposed to a contagious disease but are not yet symptomatic. This is done for the maximum known incubation period to monitor for symptoms and prevent transmission if the individual becomes infectious.
  • Both isolation and quarantine are forms of primary prevention.
  • Social distancing is a broader public health strategy that involves maintaining physical distance and avoiding large gatherings. It helps reduce the risk of disease transmission in the general population and is not limited to those who are ill or exposed.
  • Contact tracing is the process of identifying and monitoring people who have been in close contact with an infected individual. It helps identify potential secondary cases and supports further preventive actions like testing or quarantine.

question_text: Most logical and cost effective approach for control of urban rabies is
option_a: Elimination of stray dogs combined with their mass immunization
explanation:
• Elimination of stray dogs and mass immunization:
    • Stray dogs are the primary reservoirs and transmitters of rabies in urban areas.
    • Mass canine vaccination creates herd immunity, drastically reducing the risk of rabies transmission.
    • This combined strategy addresses both disease prevention and population control, making it the most cost-effective and practical method.
    • Sterilization programs often accompany this approach to reduce stray dog populations sustainably.
  • Global evidence: Countries like Mexico and Sri Lanka have shown significant reductions in rabies cases by implementing mass dog vaccination programs without resorting to indiscriminate culling.

Why Not Others?

  • B. Registration of all domestic dogs:
    • Helps identify and monitor pets but does not address the stray dog population, which is a major reservoir for rabies.
  • C. Quarantine for about one year:
    • Impractical and resource-intensive in urban settings with large stray dog populations.
    • More suitable for specific rabies-exposed animals, not as a broad strategy.
  • D. Health education:
    • Crucial for human awareness about rabies prevention and post-exposure prophylaxis but does not directly control rabies transmission in animal populations.

Key Takeaways

  • Primary reservoirs: Stray dogs are the leading sources of urban rabies transmission.
  • Cost-effective strategy: Eliminating stray dogs and vaccinating them is the most logical and impactful method for control.
  • Integrated approach: Sustainable rabies control includes dog sterilization, mass immunization, and public awareness.

question_text: Although various animals can transmit rabies, dogs are the most common source, and children are particularly affected in developing countries. Considering this, what is the most cost-effective and logical strategy to reduce the incidence of rabies?
option_a: Testing all the dogs for rabies
option_b: Reduce stray dog population and vaccinate all dogs
option_d: Increase capacity of healthcare workers for surveillance
explanation:
Explanation:

The most effective and logical strategy for reducing rabies incidence focuses on controlling the primary source of transmission (dogs), through mass vaccination and population control.

  • Mass dog vaccination: Vaccinating dogs is highly effective in breaking the transmission cycle to humans. It provides long-term protection and is a sustainable intervention in endemic regions.
  • Stray dog population control: Reducing the number of unowned or stray dogs decreases the risk of rabies exposure, especially for children, who are most vulnerable to dog bites.

This combined approach directly addresses the root cause of human rabies, making it both cost-effective and practical in resource-limited settings.

Explanation of Other Options:

Testing all the dogs for rabies (option A): While theoretically useful, testing every dog is impractical and prohibitively expensive, especially in countries with large stray populations. It does not prevent transmission; vaccination and control measures are far more effective.

Increase the laboratory facilities (option C): Enhancing diagnostic capacity helps confirm rabies cases and supports surveillance but does not prevent the disease, so it has limited impact on reducing incidence.

Increase capacity of healthcare workers for surveillance (option D): Training healthcare workers improves monitoring and reporting, but surveillance alone cannot prevent rabies cases. It complements prevention strategies but is not a standalone solution.

question_text: The median incubation period is _____________________
option_a: Time gap between onset of disease in primary and secondary cases
option_b: Time required for 50% of cases to develop disease after exposure
option_c: Time between exposure and development of first symptom
option_d: Time between exposure and diagnosis of disease
explanation:
Median Incubation Period: The median incubation period is a measure of the central tendency of the distribution of incubation periods for a particular disease. It represents the time at which half of the infected individuals who will eventually show symptoms have developed the disease after exposure to the pathogen.

 (B) Time required for 50% of cases to develop disease after exposure: This is the correct definition of the median incubation period. It indicates the time taken for half of the exposed individuals to develop symptoms of the disease.

Explanation to why other options are not correct:

(A) Time gap between onset of disease in primary and secondary cases: This option refers to the interval between the onset of disease in individuals who were directly infected (primary cases) and those who were subsequently infected from the primary cases (secondary cases). It does not specifically represent the median incubation period

(C) Time between exposure and development of first symptom: This option describes the incubation period, but it specifically refers to the time from exposure to the appearance of the initial symptoms in the infected individual, not necessarily the median value.

(D) Time between exposure and diagnosis of disease: This represents the time taken from exposure to the identification or diagnosis of the disease in the infected individual. It is influenced by various factors such as the availability of diagnostic tests, healthcare-seeking behaviour, and healthcare infrastructure. While it may provide valuable information about disease surveillance and healthcare delivery, it does not directly represent the median incubation period.

In summary, option (B) is the correct answer because it accurately defines the median incubation period as the time required for 50% of cases to develop the disease after exposure to the pathogen.

Reference - Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 107

question_text: Which of the following is the most effective prophylactic measure against cholera?
explanation:
(A) Health education:

Health education, which includes promoting awareness about proper hygiene, safe water and food practices, and sanitation measures, is considered the most effective prophylactic measure against cholera. Educating individuals and communities about the importance of handwashing with soap and water, drinking safe and treated water, and properly preparing and storing food can significantly reduce the risk of cholera transmission. Health education also emphasizes the importance of proper sanitation facilities and the safe disposal of human waste to prevent contamination of water sources.

Explanation to why other options are not correct:

(B) Vaccination:

Vaccination against cholera can provide protection against the disease, but its effectiveness as a prophylactic measure may vary depending on factors such as vaccine availability, coverage, and the specific strain of cholera circulating in a region. Cholera vaccines are primarily recommended for use in areas with endemic or epidemic cholera, during outbreaks, or for travelers visiting cholera-endemic regions. While vaccination can offer protection to individuals who receive the vaccine, it may not address underlying issues related to poor sanitation and hygiene that contribute to cholera transmission.

(C) Chemoprophylaxis:

Chemoprophylaxis involves the use of antibiotics or antimicrobial agents to prevent cholera in individuals who are at high risk of exposure or in outbreak settings. While chemoprophylaxis can be effective in preventing cholera transmission in certain situations, it is not considered the most effective prophylactic measure due to concerns such as antibiotic resistance, the potential for adverse effects, and the need for repeated dosing. Chemoprophylaxis is typically reserved for specific high-risk groups, such as household contacts of cholera patients, healthcare workers, and individuals responding to outbreaks.

(D) Early case detection:

Early case detection, while important for prompt treatment and containment of cholera outbreaks, is not a prophylactic measure in itself. Detecting and isolating cases of cholera early can help prevent further transmission of the disease through appropriate case management, contact tracing, and implementation of control measures. However, early case detection alone does not address the underlying risk factors for cholera transmission and may not prevent new cases from occurring without additional preventive measures.

In summary, health education (option A) is the most effective prophylactic measure against cholera as it addresses the root causes of transmission by promoting proper hygiene, safe water, and sanitation practices within communities. While vaccination, chemoprophylaxis, and early case detection are important components of cholera control and prevention efforts, they are not as comprehensive or universally applicable as health education in reducing the burden of cholera.

Reference - Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 276

question_text: Malignancy of lung is associated with which of the following pneumoconiosis?
explanation:
ASBESTOSIS

  • Asbestos is used in the manufacture of asbestos cement, sheets, pipes, gaskets, fire-proof textiles, etc. Exposure to this dust occurs in mining, milling and in the manufacture of asbestos products.
  • Asbestos is of two types: serpentine or chrysolite variety( white asbestos) type (i.e. hydrated magnesium silicate) and the amphibole type (hydrated silicate of iron, calcium and sodium)
  • The amphibole type occurs in different varieties, e.g., crocidolite (blue), amosite (brown), and anthophyllite (white). The blue form is more hazardous.
  • Asbestos fibres are usually from 20 to 500 µ in length and 0.5 to 50 µ in diameter.
  • Asbestos enters the body by inhalation, and fine dust may be deposited in the alveoli. The fibres are insoluble.
  •    The dust deposited in the lungs causes pulmonary fibrosis leading to respiratory insufficiency and death; carcinoma of the bronchus; mesothelioma of the pleura or peritoneum; and cancer of the gastro-intestinal tract.
  • Mesothelioma, a rare form of cancer of the pleura and peritoneum, has been shown to have a strong association with the crocidolite variety of asbestos. The disease does not usually appear until after 5 to 10 years of exposure.
  • The fibrosis in asbestosis is due to mechanical irritation, and is peribronchial, diffuse in character, and basal in location in contrast to silicosis in which the fibrosis is nodular in character and present in the upper part of the lungs.
  • Clinically the disease is characterised by dyspnea which is frequently out of proportion to the clinical signs in the lungs. In advanced cases, there may be clubbing of fingers, cardiac distress and cyanosis.
  • The sputum shows "asbestos bodies" which are asbestos fibres coated with fibrin.
  • An X-ray of the chest shows a ground-glass appearance in the lower two thirds of the lung fields. Once established, the disease is progressive even after removal of the worker from contact.
  • The preventive measures consists of:
    1. use of safer types of asbestos (chrysotile and amosite);
    2. substitution of other insulants: glass fibre, mineral wool, calcium silicate, plastic foams, etc.;
    3. rigorous dust control;
    4. periodic examination of workers; biological monitoring (clinical, X-ray, lung function), and continuing research.

question_text: Mesothelioma is characteristically associated with exposure to:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Mesothelioma is a rare but aggressive malignant tumor of the pleura and peritoneum, strongly linked to asbestos exposure.
  • Asbestos fibers → lodge in pleura/peritoneum → cause chronic irritation and genetic damage → malignant mesothelial cell proliferation.
  • Latency period: 20-40 years after exposure.
  • Asbestosis itself is a pneumoconiosis (diffuse interstitial fibrosis), but mesothelioma is the classic neoplasm associated with asbestos.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

  • Silicosis (Option A): Associated with silica dust, predisposes to tuberculosis, but not mesothelioma.
  • Coal dust (Option B): Causes coal workers' pneumoconiosis, no link with mesothelioma.
  • Berylliosis (Option D): Due to beryllium exposure (electronics, aerospace), can cause chronic granulomatous lung disease, but not mesothelioma.

question_text: Regarding the Nipah virus, which of the following statements is incorrect?
option_a: It is transmitted through bat urine
explanation:
Explanation:

The incorrect statement is that Nipah virus causes hemorrhagic fever. While severe Nipah virus infection can lead to multi-organ failure and may include gastrointestinal hemorrhage as a late and rare complication, its primary and most characteristic clinical manifestations are severe encephalitis and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). It is not classified as a viral hemorrhagic fever agent like Ebola or Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever viruses.

Explanation of other options:

It is transmitted through bat urine (Option A): The primary reservoir, fruit bats (Pteropus species), shed the virus in their urine, saliva, and excreta. Contact with these secretions or consumption of fruit/date palm sap contaminated by them is a major transmission route.

It is present in India (Option C): India has experienced multiple Nipah virus outbreaks, most notably in the states of West Bengal and Kerala (e.g., 2018, 2021, 2023).

It is an emerging infection (Option D): Nipah virus is classified as a WHO Blueprint priority pathogen and a prime example of an emerging zoonotic disease due to its outbreak potential and high case fatality rate.

Key Takeaways:

  • Nipah virus primarily causes encephalitis and respiratory illness, not hemorrhagic fever.
  • Its natural reservoir is the fruit bat.
  • It is a significant emerging public health threat in South and Southeast Asia, including India.

Reference:

  1. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - Nipah Virus.
  2. World Health Organization (WHO) - Nipah Virus Infection.

question_text: A 30-year-old patient presents with hypopigmented patches, loss of cold sensation followed by loss of hot, touch, and pain sensations, along with a palpable, thickened ulnar nerve. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of clinical findings in this patient is a classic presentation of leprosy (also known as Hansen's disease), which is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium leprae.

The key diagnostic features are:

  • Hypopigmented Patches with Sensory Loss: One of the cardinal signs of leprosy is the presence of skin lesions that have a definite loss of sensation.
  • Specific Pattern of Sensory Loss: The disease process affects nerve fibers sequentially, typically starting with the small, unmyelinated fibers that transmit temperature sensation (cold first, then hot), followed by the fibers for pain, and finally the larger fibers for touch.
  • Thickened Peripheral Nerves: M. leprae has a predilection for peripheral nerves, causing inflammation and thickening. The ulnar nerve is one of the most commonly affected nerves, and its palpability is a hallmark physical finding.

This triad of skin lesions, sensory loss, and thickened peripheral nerves is highly specific for leprosy.

Explanation of other options:

TB (Option A): While caused by another mycobacterium (M. tuberculosis), tuberculosis typically presents with constitutional symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss) and organ-specific signs, most commonly affecting the lungs (persistent cough). It does not cause this characteristic pattern of sensory loss and nerve thickening.

HIV (Option C): HIV infection leads to immunodeficiency. While peripheral neuropathy can be a complication of HIV or its treatment, it does not typically present with hypopigmented anesthetic skin patches and the classic sensory loss pattern described.

Candida (Option D): Candida usually causes mucocutaneous infections (oral thrush, vaginal candidiasis) or disseminated infection in immunocompromised individuals. It is not associated with anesthetic patches or palpable peripheral nerves.

Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7058852/

question_text: Practical Approach to Lung health(PAL) includes all except
explanation:
The Practical Approach to Lung Health (PAL) strategy is a comprehensive approach developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) to address common respiratory conditions effectively. It aims to provide practical guidance for healthcare providers in managing lung diseases at the primary healthcare level.

d. Carcinoma lung: Carcinoma of the lung, commonly referred to as lung cancer, is not typically included in the Practical Approach to Lung Health (PAL) strategy. While lung cancer is a significant respiratory condition, PAL primarily focuses on common respiratory diseases that can be effectively managed at the primary healthcare level. Lung cancer diagnosis and treatment often require specialized interventions beyond the scope of primary healthcare, such as advanced imaging, biopsy, oncology consultations, and specialized treatments like surgery, chemotherapy, or radiotherapy.

Explanation to why other options are not correct:

a. TB (Tuberculosis): Tuberculosis is a major global health concern, and it is included in the Practical Approach to Lung Health (PAL) strategy. PAL provides guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment, and management of tuberculosis, considering its significant burden on public health worldwide.

b. Bronchial Asthma: Bronchial asthma, a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways, is also included in the PAL strategy. PAL offers guidance on the diagnosis, treatment, and management of asthma, aiming to improve the quality of life for individuals affected by this condition.

c. COPD (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease): COPD, a progressive lung disease characterized by airflow limitation, is a key focus of the PAL strategy. PAL provides recommendations for the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of COPD, aiming to reduce its impact on individuals and healthcare systems.

e. Pneumonia: Pneumonia, an infection that inflames the air sacs in one or both lungs, is another condition included in the PAL strategy. PAL offers guidance on the diagnosis, treatment, and management of pneumonia, emphasizing early detection and appropriate treatment to prevent complications.

In summary, the Practical Approach to Lung Health (PAL) strategy includes TB, Bronchial Asthma, COPD, and Pneumonia but typically does not include Carcinoma lung (lung cancer) due to its complexity and the need for specialized care beyond the primary healthcare level. Therefore, option (d) Carcinoma lung is the correct answer as the exception in the PAL strategy.

Reference - Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 486

question_text: S in the SAFE strategy of trachoma stands for?
explanation:
• The "S" in the SAFE strategy for trachoma stands for Surgery. The SAFE strategy is a comprehensive approach to control and eliminate trachoma, which is a major cause of blindness. It includes:
    • Surgery (tertiary prevention) to correct advanced stages like trichiasis and entropion.
    • Antibiotics (secondary prevention) to treat and prevent infection.
    • Facial cleanliness (primary prevention) to reduce the transmission of the infection.
    • Environmental changes (primordial prevention) to reduce the spread of disease through improved sanitation.

SAFE Strategy Components:

  • S: Surgery - Tertiary prevention for correcting trichiasis and entropion.
  • A: Antibiotics - Azithromycin (single dose) or tetracycline ointment for preventing and treating the infection.
  • F: Facial hygiene - Primary prevention through promoting clean faces to reduce transmission.
  • E: Environmental improvement - Improving sanitation and eliminating flies that transmit the disease.

Key Takeaways:

  • The "S" in the SAFE strategy stands for Surgery, which is crucial for advanced stages of trachoma.
  • The SAFE strategy combines surgery, antibiotics, facial cleanliness, and environmental changes to control and prevent trachoma.

question_text: A 25-year-old patient with a known history of rheumatic heart disease (RHD) presents for a routine follow-up. As part of their management, they receive a regular intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin. Which level of prevention does this intervention represent?
explanation:
Explanation:

The administration of benzathine penicillin to a patient with established rheumatic heart disease is a classic example of Secondary Prevention.

  • The patient already has a diagnosed disease (RHD).
  • The goal of benzathine penicillin in this context is not to prevent the initial streptococcal infection (which would be primary prevention) but to prevent recurrent streptococcal infections.
  • Preventing these recurrences is crucial to halt the progression of the existing valvular heart disease and avert serious complications like heart failure, arrhythmias, or the need for valve surgery.
  • Secondary prevention focuses precisely on this: early detection and prompt intervention in a disease that is already present to prevent complications and progression.

Explanation of other options:

Primordial Prevention (Option A): Primordial prevention aims to prevent the emergence and establishment of risk factors themselves (e.g., promoting healthy lifestyles in communities to avoid obesity and poverty, which are risk factors for rheumatic fever). It occurs before any disease process begins.

Primary Prevention (Option B): Primary prevention would involve measures to prevent the first occurrence of rheumatic fever in a healthy individual, such as adequate treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis with antibiotics. The patient in the question already has the sequela of rheumatic fever, which is RHD.

Tertiary Prevention (Option D): Tertiary prevention comes into play when a disease has already caused significant impairment. It focuses on rehabilitation and minimizing disability (e.g., cardiac rehabilitation after valve replacement surgery for advanced RHD). The penicillin injection is aimed at preventing this advanced stage, not managing it.

Key Takeaways:

  • Secondary Prevention targets early, existing disease to stop its progression.
  • In RHD, benzathine penicillin is secondary prevention because it treats the consequence of the disease (the risk of progression) after the primary disease (rheumatic fever) has already caused damage.
  • Distinguish this from primary prevention (preventing the initial rheumatic fever) and tertiary prevention (managing heart failure from severe RHD).

question_text: Legal steps to ban the entry of tobacco products in a tribal area where the community has no exposure to tobacco is
explanation:
Primordial prevention involves addressing social, economic, and environmental factors that influence health behaviours before they occur.

Explanation for why the other options are incorrect:

b. Primary: Primary prevention typically involves interventions aimed at preventing the onset of disease by addressing risk factors or promoting health behaviours. Banning the entry of tobacco products in a community with no exposure to tobacco would not be considered primary prevention because there is no existing disease or risk factor to prevent.

c. Secondary: Secondary prevention involves early detection and treatment of disease to prevent its progression or complications. Banning the entry of tobacco products does not involve detecting or treating existing disease.

d. Tertiary: Tertiary prevention involves interventions aimed at managing and reducing the impact of existing disease or disability. Banning the entry of tobacco products does not relate to managing existing disease or disability.

Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 48

question_text: Which of the following is an example of disability limitation for polio?
option_a: Polio immunization drives for infants to reduce the occurrence
option_b: Arranging for schooling for a child suffering from residual polio paralysis
option_c: Resting the affected limbs due to polio in neutral position
option_d: Providing calipers for walking to patients affected by polio
explanation:
Disability limitation for polio involves measures aimed at preventing or minimizing the impact of polio-related disabilities on individuals

(C) Resting the affected limbs due to polio in a neutral position:

This option directly addresses the physical aspect of disability limitation for polio. Resting the affected limbs in a neutral position helps prevent contractures and deformities by maintaining proper alignment and reducing stress on the muscles and joints. It is an important rehabilitation measure to preserve functional ability and prevent further disability.

Explanation to why other options are not correct:

(A) Polio immunization drives for infants to reduce the occurrence:

This option represents a preventive measure rather than a disability limitation strategy. Polio immunization drives aim to prevent polio infection altogether by providing vaccination to infants, thereby reducing the occurrence of the disease. While immunization is essential for preventing disability due to polio, it falls under the category of primary prevention rather than disability limitation.

(B) Arranging for schooling for a child suffering from residual polio paralysis:

This option addresses the social aspect of disability but does not directly limit or minimize the disability caused by polio. While schooling is important for the overall well-being and integration of children with disabilities, it focuses on social inclusion rather than directly limiting the disability itself.

(D) Providing calipers for walking to patients affected by polio:

While providing assistive devices such as calipers can improve mobility and independence for individuals with polio-related disabilities, it falls under the category of rehabilitation rather than disability limitation. Calipers and other assistive devices help individuals compensate for their disabilities but do not directly limit or minimize the disability itself.

In summary, resting the affected limbs due to polio in a neutral position (option C) is the most appropriate example of disability limitation because it directly addresses the physical aspect of disability by preventing contractures and deformities. Options (A), (B), and (D) represent important interventions for polio prevention, social inclusion, and rehabilitation, respectively, but they do not directly limit or minimize the disability caused by polio.

Reference - Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 244

question_text: A patient is resistant to Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Ofloxacin and Kanamycin. What type of resistance is being shown by the patient?
explanation:
CLASSIFICATION BASED ON DRUG RESISTANCE

  1. Mono-resistance: Resistance to one first-line anti-TB drug only.
  2. Poly drug resistance: Resistance to more than one first line anti-TB drug (other than both isoniazid and rifampicin).
  3. Multidrug resistance: Resistance to at least both isoniazid and rifampicin.
  4. Extensive drug resistance: Resistance to any fluoroquinolone and Resistance to atleast one additional group A drug- i.e either Bedaquiline or Linezolid or both.
  5. Rifampicin resistance: Resistance to rifampicin detected using phenotypic or genotypic methods, with or without resistance to other anti-TB drugs. It includes any resistance to rifampicin, whether mono-resistance, multidrug resistance, poly drug resistance or extensive drug resistance.
  6. Pre XDR TB: MDR/RR TB + any one fluoroquinolone resistance.
    Prevention of Drug Resistance : Since incomplete, inadequate and irregular treatment is the main cause of drug resistance, this can be prevented by
    1. Treatment with two or more drugs in combination
    2. Using drugs to which the bacteria are sensitive, and
    3. Ensuring that the treatment is complete, adequate and regular.
  7. Former definition of Extensive drug resistant TB: Resistance to any fluoroquinolone and at least one of three second-line injectable drugs (capreomycin, kanamycin and amikacin), in addition to multidrug resistance.

question_text: What health hazards are sugarcane factory workers potentially exposed to?
explanation:
Explanation:

Bagassosis is a lung disease caused by inhaling moldy sugarcane dust. Sugarcane bagasse, the fibrous residue left after juice extraction, can become moldy under certain conditions. Workers handling or processing this bagasse are at risk of developing bagassosis due to inhaling mold spores.

Bagassosis

  • Caused by inhaling sugarcane fibers, also seen in the cardboard and paper industries.
  • The fungus responsible is Thermoactinomyces sacchari.
  • First reported in India by Ganguly and Pal.
  • X-ray shows mottling in lung fields.
  • Control measures include maintaining moisture content above 20% and spraying bagasse with 2% propionic acid.

Explanation for other options:

Anthracosis (Option A): Lung disease caused by inhaling coal dust.

Siderosis (Option B): Caused by inhaling iron dust or particles.

Byssinosis (Option D): Also called "brown lung disease," linked to dust from textile fibers like cotton, flax, or hemp.

Learning Objective:

Occupational lung diseases like these are notifiable under various national laws such as the Factories Act (1976) and Mines Act (1952). These regulations require reporting of confirmed or suspected cases to enable prevention, protection, and investigation of working conditions.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7724370/#:~:text=Bird%20Fancier's%20Lung%20is%20a,common%20causes%20of%20hypersensitivity%20pneumonitis.

question_text: Avahan program is a combined prevention approach for
explanation:
The Avahan program is a large-scale HIV prevention initiative implemented by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation in partnership with various governmental and non-governmental organizations in India. The program primarily focuses on HIV prevention among high-risk populations, such as female sex workers, men who have sex with men, transgender individuals, and injecting drug users.

Explanation to why other options are not correct:

a. Malaria: The Avahan program does not address malaria prevention. Malaria is a mosquito-borne infectious disease caused by parasites of the Plasmodium genus, whereas Avahan primarily focuses on HIV prevention strategies, including condom promotion, HIV testing and counselling, behaviour change communication, and linkage to HIV care and treatment services.

c. TB (Tuberculosis): Although tuberculosis (TB) is another significant public health concern in India, the Avahan program is specifically designed to address HIV prevention, not TB prevention or control. TB and HIV often coexist due to overlapping risk factors and immunosuppression caused by HIV infection, but Avahan primarily targets HIV prevention efforts.

d. Kala-azar (Visceral Leishmaniasis): Kala-azar, also known as visceral leishmaniasis, is a parasitic disease transmitted by sandflies. While Kala-azar is endemic in some regions of India, particularly Bihar, the Avahan program does not focus on preventing or controlling this disease. Instead, it concentrates on HIV prevention efforts among key populations at higher risk of HIV transmission.

In summary, the Avahan program is a combined prevention approach specifically targeted at HIV prevention among high-risk populations in India. It does not address malaria, tuberculosis, or kala-azar. Therefore, option (b) HIV is the correct answer.

Reference:RESPECT-implementation-guide-Programme-summary-Avahan-en.pdf (unwomen.org)

question_text: A group organized a mass gathering to promote awareness about hand hygiene. What is the correct sequence in the adoption of a health-related practice?
explanation:
Explanation:

The adoption of a new health practice follows a sequence based on the Diffusion of Innovation Theory, which describes how individuals accept and implement new behaviors. The correct sequence is:

  • Awareness - People are first informed about the practice (e.g., the importance of handwashing).
  • Interest - They develop curiosity and want to learn more.
  • Evaluation - They assess whether the practice is beneficial and feasible for them.
  • Adoption - They accept and implement the new practice into their daily routine.

Example for Handwashing Awareness Campaign:

  • Awareness - Conducting mass gatherings, posters, and demonstrations about handwashing.
  • Interest - People start asking questions and showing curiosity about proper techniques.
  • Evaluation - They compare the benefits (prevention of diseases) and the feasibility of following the practice.
  • Adoption - They start washing hands regularly as a habit.

This stepwise process ensures behavioral change and long-term practice adoption in public health interventions.

Explanation of other options:

Adoption, evaluation, awareness, interest (Option A): This sequence is incorrect, as awareness and interest must come before evaluation and adoption for behavioral change to occur.

Evaluation, awareness, interest, adoption (Option B): Awareness and interest are the initial steps in adopting a new practice, and evaluation typically follows them.

Interest, evaluation, adoption, awareness (Option C): Awareness is the first step, followed by interest, then evaluation, and finally adoption. This sequence is out of order.

Key Takeaways:

  • The correct sequence for the adoption of a health practice is Awareness → Interest → Evaluation → Adoption.
  • This structured approach supports effective public health campaigns aimed at behavior change.

question_text: Which of the following options can be used to treat Kesari dal toxicity?
explanation:
Explanation:

Lathyrism is a paralytic disease caused by consuming large amounts of Lathyrus sativus (Kesari dhal), which contains the neurotoxin Beta oxalyl amino alanine (BOAA).

Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) plays a crucial role in prevention and treatment.

Daily supplementation of 500-1000 mg of vitamin C can help repair nerve damage and prevent progression of neurolathyrism.

Animal studies have shown vitamin C effectively reduces the toxic effects of Lathyrus toxin.

Including adequate vitamin C in the diet is a key protective measure, especially where

Kesari dhal consumption cannot be avoided. Vitamin C acts as an antioxidant that counters the neurotoxic effects of the toxin.

Explanation for other options:

Sodium bicarbonate (Option A): This is incorrect, as sodium bicarbonate is primarily used to manage metabolic acidosis and does not play a role in the treatment of Kesari dal toxicity.

Vitamin A (Option B): This option is incorrect because, although Vitamin A is important for maintaining eye health and immune function, it is not specifically indicated for managing toxicity caused by Kesari dal.

IV immunoglobulin (Option D): This is not the correct choice, since IV immunoglobulin is typically used in the treatment of autoimmune disorders and certain infections, rather than in cases of Kesari dal toxicity.

question_text: Recommended dose of folic acid during pregnancy is
explanation:
Option D: 500 mcg/day:

  • 500 mcg/day is the recommended dose of folic acid for pregnant women by several health organizations, including the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the World Health Organization (WHO).
  • This higher dose is recommended to ensure sufficient folate levels for preventing neural tube defects and supporting overall foetal development.
  • Adequate folic acid intake during pregnancy is crucial, especially during the early weeks when neural tube formation occurs, to reduce the risk of birth defects affecting the brain and spinal cord.

Why the other options are not correct:

Option A: 200 mcg/day:

  • 200 mcg/day is a lower dose of folic acid that may not provide adequate supplementation during pregnancy.
  • The recommended daily intake of folic acid for pregnant women is higher to support the increased need for folate during pregnancy, particularly for preventing neural tube defects in the developing foetus.

Option B: 300 mcg/day:

  • Similarly, 300 mcg/day is a relatively low dose of folic acid for pregnant women.
  • While some women may require this dose for preconception health or during early pregnancy, it may not be sufficient for all pregnant women, especially those at higher risk of neural tube defects.

Option C: 400 mcg/day:

  • 400 mcg/day is a commonly recommended dose of folic acid for most pregnant women, particularly in the early stages of pregnancy.
  • While this dose may be sufficient for many women, some health organizations and experts recommend higher doses, such as 500 mcg/day, to ensure adequate folate intake for optimal pregnancy outcomes.

In summary, while options A, B, and C may be appropriate for some women in specific circumstances, option D (500 mcg/day) is the recommended dose of folic acid for most pregnant women to ensure optimal pregnancy outcomes and reduce the risk of neural tube defects in the developing foetus.

Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 603

question_text: Recommended dose of folic acid during lactation is
explanation:
Option D: 500 mcg/day:

  • 500 mcg/day is the recommended dose of folic acid for lactating women by several health organizations, including the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the World Health Organization (WHO).
  • This higher dose is recommended to ensure sufficient folate levels in breast milk, which is essential for the infant's growth, development, and overall health.
  • Adequate folic acid intake during lactation helps prevent folate deficiency in both the mother and the infant and supports optimal breastfeeding outcomes.

Why the other options are not correct:

Option A: 200 mcg/day:

  • 200 mcg/day is a lower dose of folic acid that may not provide adequate supplementation during lactation.
  • The recommended daily intake of folic acid for lactating women is higher to support the increased need for folate during breastfeeding, which is essential for the health and development of both the mother and the infant.

Option B: 300 mcg/day:

  • Similarly, 300 mcg/day is a relatively low dose of folic acid for lactating women.
  • While this dose may be sufficient for some women in specific circumstances, it may not meet the increased demand for folate during lactation, especially for those with higher requirements.

Option C: 400 mcg/day:

  • 400 mcg/day is a commonly recommended dose of folic acid for most adults, including non-pregnant and non-lactating individuals.
  • While this dose may be appropriate for general health maintenance, it may not provide adequate folate intake for lactating women who have increased nutritional needs during breastfeeding.

In summary, while options A, B, and C may be appropriate for some individuals in specific circumstances, option D (500 mcg/day) is the recommended dose of folic acid for most lactating women to ensure optimal maternal and infant health during breastfeeding.

Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 603

question_text: IMCI was taken to prevent morbidity and mortality from all except
explanation:
d. Neonatal tetanus:

- Neonatal tetanus is caused by the bacterium Clostridium tetani and typically occurs through contamination of the umbilical stump. While neonatal tetanus is a serious and potentially fatal disease, IMCI primarily focuses on illnesses affecting children beyond the neonatal period (i.e., beyond the first 28 days of life). Therefore, neonatal tetanus prevention and management fall outside the scope of IMCI.

Why the other options are not correct:

The Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) strategy was developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) to address the leading causes of morbidity and mortality among children under the age of five in low-resource settings. IMCI aims to reduce illness, disability, and death associated with the following major childhood diseases:

a. Malaria:

- Malaria is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality among children in many tropical and subtropical regions. IMCI includes guidelines for the prevention, diagnosis, and management of malaria in children.

b. Malnutrition:

- Malnutrition, including both undernutrition and overnutrition, contributes significantly to childhood morbidity and mortality. IMCI emphasizes the assessment and management of nutritional status, including the identification and treatment of malnourished children.

c. Otitis media:

- Otitis media, or middle ear infection, is a common childhood illness that can lead to complications if left untreated. IMCI provides guidance on the diagnosis and management of otitis media in children.

In summary, option D is the correct answer because neonatal tetanus prevention and management are not specifically addressed within the IMCI strategy, which primarily targets common childhood illnesses occurring after the neonatal period. Options A, B, and C represent significant targets of the IMCI strategy, as they are leading causes of childhood morbidity and mortality in low-resource settings.

Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 655

question_text: People of a community are consuming Khesari Dal for last few years. Lathyrism prevention step in community are all; EXCEPT:
explanation:
Lathyrism is a neurological disorder caused by the consumption of excessive amounts of the legume Lathyrus sativus, commonly known as Khesari Dal. It primarily affects the nervous system, leading to irreversible paralysis of the lower limbs.

Why the other options are not correct:

b. Ban the crop: Banning the cultivation or consumption of Khesari Dal is a crucial preventive measure to reduce the incidence of lathyrism in the community. By prohibiting the cultivation and sale of the crop, individuals are prevented from consuming it, thereby reducing the risk of lathyrism.

c. Vitamin C: Vitamin C supplementation may help reduce the severity of lathyrism symptoms and provide some degree of protection against the neurotoxic effects of Lathyrus sativus consumption. However, it is not the most effective preventive measure compared to banning the crop or toxin removal.

d. Toxin removal: Implementing methods to remove or detoxify the neurotoxic compounds present in Khesari Dal is another important preventive measure. Techniques such as soaking, boiling, or fermentation can help reduce the levels of these toxins, making the dal safer for consumption.

Option a, DEC (diethylcarbamazine), is not relevant to the prevention of lathyrism. DEC is an anthelmintic medication used primarily to treat lymphatic filariasis, a parasitic disease caused by filarial worms. It is not indicated for the prevention or treatment of lathyrism.

In summary, while options b, c, and d are all effective preventive measures against lathyrism, option a (DEC) is not relevant to this condition and is therefore the correct answer as an exception.

Reference : Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 759

question_text: The infectivity of a disease is best measured by which of the following?
explanation:
Explanation:

Infectivity is defined as the ability of an infectious agent to enter, multiply, and establish an infection in a susceptible host. While infectivity is an intrinsic property of the agent, it is quantified in a population using the Secondary Attack Rate (SAR).

The SAR measures the frequency of new cases of a disease among the contacts of a known primary case. It is calculated as:

SAR = (No. of new cases among contacts / Total no. of susceptible contacts) x 100

A high secondary attack rate implies a high infectivity of the agent, as it demonstrates the agent's efficiency in spreading from an infected individual to their susceptible contacts.

Explanation of other options:

Incubation period (Option A): This is the time interval between the initial invasion by the infectious agent and the appearance of the first sign or symptom of the disease. It reflects the agent's replication time, not its ability to spread.

Serial Interval (Option B): This is the time gap between the onset of symptoms in the primary case and the onset of symptoms in a secondary case infected by that primary case. It is a measure of the speed of transmission in a chain of infection.

Case fatality rate (Option D): This measures the severity or virulence of a disease, not its infectivity. It measures the proportion of individuals who die from a particular disease compared to the total number of individuals diagnosed with the disease.

Key Takeaway:

question_text: Which of the options below aids in determining the severity of a disease?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Case Fatality Rate (CFR) is a key indicator of disease severity. It represents the proportion of individuals diagnosed with a specific disease who die from it within a specified period.

A higher CFR indicates a more severe or lethal disease, as it reflects the disease's "killing power" among those who contract it.

Explanation of other options:

Proportional mortality rate (Option A): This indicates what proportion of all deaths in a population is due to a specific cause. It reflects the overall burden of a disease on mortality but does not directly measure its severity among the sick.

Incidence (Option B): This measures the rate of occurrence of new cases of a disease in a population over a period. It indicates the risk of contracting the disease, not its lethality.

Prevalence (Option D): This measures the total number of existing cases (both new and old) of a disease in a population at a specific point in time. It reflects the overall disease burden but not its severity.

Key Takeaways:

  • Case Fatality Rate (CFR) is the primary measure for assessing the severity or lethality of a disease.
  • Incidence measures risk of getting the disease; Prevalence measures the total burden of the disease.

question_text: Bio-terrorism group A - agent is
explanation:
Anthrax is caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis and is considered a Category A bioterrorism agent by the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in the United States. Category A agents are those that pose the highest risk to national security because they can be easily disseminated or transmitted from person to person, result in high mortality rates, and have the potential for major public health impact.

Explanation for why not the other options:

A. Q fever:

  • Q fever is caused by the bacterium Coxiella burnetii and is not typically considered a bioterrorism agent. It is not as easily transmissible as anthrax and does not have the same potential for widespread impact.

B. Typhus fever:

  • Typhus fever is caused by Rickettsia species bacteria and is not typically considered a bioterrorism agent. While it can cause serious illness, it is not as easily disseminated or associated with intentional acts of bioterrorism as anthrax.

D. Brucellosis:

  • Brucellosis is caused by bacteria of the genus Brucella and is not typically considered a bioterrorism agent. While it can cause serious illness, it is not as easily transmissible or associated with intentional acts of bioterrorism as anthrax.

Reference :Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine,27th Edition ,Page no.:984

question_text: Proportional mortality rate is ?
option_a: Number of death due to a particular cause
option_b: Number of death during that year
option_c: Number of death in one month
explanation: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Number of death due to a particular cause Proportional mortality rate (ratio) Proportional mortality rate measures the proportion of total death due to specific cause or proportion of deaths in a particular age group. It is defined as "number of deaths due to a particular cause (or in specific age group) per 100 total deaths". It is the 'simplest measure of estimating the burden of disears' in the community. It is a useful 'health Status indicator'; indicates magnitude of preventable mortality. It is used when population data is not available. It does not indicate the risk of members of population contracting or dying from the disease.

question_text: A study based in Delhi was conducted in 2014 with a group of 5000 to 6000 people to study the occurrence of a disease till 2024. What type of study is this?
explanation:
Explanation:

A prospective cohort study follows a group of individuals (a cohort) over a period of time to observe the occurrence of a disease.

  • In this case, the study began in 2014 and tracked 5,000 to 6,000 people until 2024, making it a longitudinal study where participants were observed for disease occurrence over time.
  • This type of study helps establish causal relationships by identifying risk factors and following participants before they develop the disease.

Explanation of other options:

Case-control study (Option A): Compares people with the disease (cases) and without the disease (controls) retrospectively, rather than following a cohort over time.

Ecological study (Option C): Studies populations or groups rather than individuals and uses aggregated data, not individual follow-ups.

Cross-sectional study (Option D): Examines a population at a single point in time, rather than tracking individuals over several years.

Key Takeaways:

A prospective cohort study tracks individuals over time to observe disease development, making it the correct choice for this study conducted from 2014 to 2024.

question_text: A researcher is studying the difference in the incidence of asthma in children who are exposed to second-hand smoke and those who are not. If he wishes to express the additional incidence of asthma in the exposed children as a percentage, which of the following should he use?
explanation:
Explanation:

The researcher needs to express the additional incidence of disease specifically in the exposed group. This is precisely what the Attributable Risk (AR) measures.

Attributable Risk is the difference in incidence rates between the exposed and unexposed groups. It quantifies the disease burden that can be attributed solely to the exposure.

This value (AR) can be expressed as a percentage of the incidence in the exposed group, which is known as the Attributable Risk Percent (AR%). This directly answers the question of what percentage of the disease in the exposed group is due to the exposure.

Explanation of other options:

Relative risk (Option B): This is a ratio (not a difference) that tells us how many times more likely the exposed group is to develop the disease compared to the unexposed group. It does not directly quantify the "additional incidence."

Population attributable risk (Option C): This measures the proportion of disease in the entire population (exposed and unexposed) attributable to the exposure. The question is specifically about the "exposed children," not the whole population.

Odds ratio (Option D): This is a measure of association used primarily in case-control studies where incidence cannot be calculated. It approximates the relative risk but is not a direct measure of additional incidence.

Key Takeaways:

  • Attributable Risk (AR): Measures the absolute excess risk of disease in the exposed group.
  • Attributable Risk Percent (AR%): The proportion of disease in the exposed group that is due to the exposure, expressed as a percentage.

question_text: A doctor is doing a Clinical trial in which there is error in clinical overreporting of disease in one group. The Selection bias removal can be done by
explanation:
RANDOMIZATION

  • Randomization is a statistical procedure by which the participants are allocated into groups usually called "study" and "control'' groups, to receive or not to receive an experimental preventive or therapeutic procedure, maneuver or intervention.
  • Randomization is an attempt to eliminate ''bias" and allow for comparability.
  • Randomization is the "heart" of a control trial. It will give the greatest confidence that the groups are comparable so that "like can be compared with like".
  • Selection of study group (Experimental group): It is the actual population (or volunteers) derived from the reference population randomly, participating in the experiment, still retaining the same characteristics as the reference population. Randomization eliminates bias and allows comparability. The study group receives the intervention (experimental procedure)
  • The study group should fulfil the following three criteria:
    1. It should be 'Representative' of the reference population.
    2. They must give 'informed consent', after being fully informed about the procedure and possible dangers of the trial.
    3. They must be 'Susceptible' to the disease under study. (i.e. qualified or eligible)
    4. Example: Suppose the trial is on the effect of a new drug for Anemia, the volunteers must be anemic.
  • Selection of control group: Another group of the same size as that of the study group is selected at random from the reference population, maintaining the similar characteristics (e.g. age, sex, occupation, literacy level, income, etc.) as that of the study group but they do not receive intervention.
  • It ensures that the investigator has no control over allocation of participants to either study or control group, thus eliminating what is known as "selection bias". In other words, by random allocation, every individual gets an equal chance of being allocated into either group or any of the trial groups.
  • It is crucial that both the groups should be alike with regard to certain variables or characteristics that might affect the outcome of the experiment (e.g., age, sex), the entire study population can be stratified into sub-groups according to the variable, and individuals within each sub-group can then be randomly allocated into study and control groups.
  • Randomization is best done by using a table of random numbers.
  • The essential difference between a randomized controlled trial and an analytical study is that in the latter, there is no randomization because a differentiation into diseased and non-diseased (exposed or non-exposed) groups has already taken place. The only option left to ensure comparability in analytical studies is by matching.
  • Randomization 'removes both confounding and bias'- Randomisation is SUPERIOR to both Matching and Blinding.

KEY TAKE AWAY

question_text:
The following are the disease frequencies in a population. Based on the number of cases, which of the following is the correct match?
Disease 1- number of cases last week= 42, this week=43
Disease 2- number of cases last week= 2, this week= 42
Disease 3- number of cases last year= 6, this year= 1
explanation:
Analyze each disease's frequency and match it with the correct term:

Disease 1:

Number of cases last week: 42

Number of cases this week: 43

The number of cases for Disease 1 shows a slight increase from last week to this week, but it remains within a relatively consistent range. This pattern suggests that Disease 1 is endemic to the population. Endemic diseases have a consistent presence within a population over time.

Disease 2:

Number of cases last week: 2 Number of cases this week: 42

The number of cases for Disease 2 has increased dramatically from last week to this week. Such a significant increase in cases within a short period indicates an outbreak or epidemic. Therefore, Disease 2 is indicative of an epidemic.

Disease 3:

Number of cases last year: 6

Number of cases this year: 1

Disease 3 shows a substantial decrease in cases from last year to this year. This pattern suggests that Disease 3 is sporadic, as it occurs infrequently and irregularly within the population.

Explanation to why other options are not correct:

(A) Pandemic, endemic, sporadic:

This option does not match the given diseases correctly. Disease 2, which exhibits a sudden increase in cases, is more indicative of an epidemic than a pandemic. Additionally, Disease 3, with its decrease in cases from last year to this year, is more characteristic of a sporadic disease rather than an endemic one.

(B) Sporadic, endemic, epidemic:

This option incorrectly orders the diseases. Disease 2, with its sudden increase in cases, is indicative of an epidemic rather than sporadic. Disease 1, with its consistent number of cases over time, is more indicative of an endemic disease rather than sporadic.

(D) Endemic, sporadic, epidemic:

This option incorrectly orders the diseases as well. Disease 2, with its sudden increase in cases, is indicative of an epidemic rather than sporadic. Disease 3, with its decrease in cases from last year to this year, is more characteristic of a sporadic disease rather than endemic.

In summary, option (C) correctly matches the diseases with their respective terms: Disease 1 is endemic, Disease 2 is epidemic, and Disease 3 is sporadic.

Reference - Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 101

question_text: A disease that is imported to an area from another is called _________________
explanation:
(D) Exotic disease:

Exotic disease refers to a disease that is introduced into a new area or population from outside sources. These diseases are not native to the affected area and are typically brought in through international travel, trade, or movement of infected individuals or animals. Exotic diseases can have significant impacts on local ecosystems, economies, and public health.

Explanation to why other options are not correct:

(A) Epornithic disease:

Epornithic refers to diseases that primarily affect birds. It doesn't specifically describe a disease that is imported to an area from another.

(B) Enzootic disease:

Enzootic refers to diseases that are constantly present within an animal population or ecosystem. These diseases are maintained within a specific animal population without the need for external introductions. While enzootic diseases can spread to new areas, the term itself doesn't specifically imply that the disease is imported from another area.

(C) Epizootic disease:

Epizootic refers to a sudden and widespread outbreak of disease within an animal population, similar to an epidemic in humans. Like enzootic diseases, epizootic diseases can spread to new areas, but the term does not specifically indicate that the disease is imported from another area.

In summary, option (D) Exotic disease is the correct answer as it specifically describes a disease that is imported to an area from another, aligning with the definition provided in the question. The other options (A), (B), and (C) do not specifically denote diseases that are imported from other areas.

Reference - Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 101

question_text: Which of the following carriers shed the organism for indefinite period?
explanation:
Carriers are individuals who harbour and can transmit infectious agents without showing symptoms of the disease themselves.

(C) Chronic carriers: Chronic carriers are individuals who continue to harbor and shed infectious agents for an indefinite or prolonged period, often for years or even a lifetime. These carriers typically have a persistent infection that persists despite treatment or without causing significant symptoms. Chronic carriers are particularly concerning because they can unknowingly spread the infection to others over an extended period.

Explanation to why other options are not correct:

(A) Convalescent carriers: Convalescent carriers are individuals who have recovered from an infectious disease but continue to shed the organism for a limited period during the recovery phase. They may shed the organism for a short time after their symptoms have resolved, but this shedding typically ceases once they fully recover.

(B) Healthy carriers: Healthy carriers are individuals who harbor and shed infectious agents without ever developing symptoms of the disease themselves. They can continue to shed the organism for an extended period, but it is not necessarily indefinite. Healthy carriers may eventually clear the infection naturally or with treatment.

(D) Pseudo carriers: Pseudo carriers are individuals who test positive for the presence of an infectious agent but do not actually harbor the organism or pose a risk of transmission. Pseudo positivity may occur due to factors such as contamination during sample collection or laboratory error. Pseudo carriers do not shed the organism because they are not truly infected.

Given that chronic carriers are the ones who continue to shed the organism for an indefinite or prolonged period, the correct answer is (C) Chronic carriers. They represent a significant public health concern due to their potential to sustain transmission of the infection over time.

Reference - Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 104

question_text: Disease occurrence in a haphazard manner is called _____________
explanation:
(A) Sporadic:

Sporadic refers to the occurrence of a disease in a random or irregular manner, with isolated cases or small outbreaks happening unpredictably. These cases are not connected to each other in terms of time or location, and there is no consistent pattern of transmission. Sporadic diseases occur infrequently and may not follow any discernible trend or geographic clustering.

Explanation to why other options are not correct:

(B) Pandemic:

Pandemic refers to the widespread occurrence of a disease across multiple countries or continents, affecting a large proportion of the global population. Pandemics involve the rapid spread of a disease, often facilitated by international travel and trade. Unlike sporadic diseases, pandemics involve a coordinated and sustained transmission of the disease on a global scale.

(C) Endemic:

Endemic refers to the constant presence of a disease within a specific geographic area or population group. Endemic diseases persistently occur at a relatively stable level within their defined area or group, without necessarily spreading beyond those boundaries. Unlike sporadic diseases, which occur irregularly, endemic diseases are consistently present within their endemic areas.

(D) Opportunistic:

Opportunistic infections are those caused by pathogens that take advantage of weakened immune systems in hosts, such as individuals with immunodeficiency disorders or undergoing medical treatments that suppress the immune system. Opportunistic infections typically occur in individuals who are vulnerable due to underlying health conditions or medical interventions, rather than spreading haphazardly like sporadic diseases.

In summary, option (A) Sporadic is the correct answer as it specifically describes the occurrence of a disease in a haphazard or irregular manner, with isolated cases or small outbreaks happening unpredictably, without any consistent pattern of transmission or geographic clustering.

Reference - Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 101

question_text: What is the likely cause of acute leg swelling and loose stools in a 40-year-old female patient, given that her family members exhibit similar symptoms and mustard oil is commonly used in their diet?
explanation:
Explanation:

Sanguinarine is the toxic alkaloid found in argemone oil, which contaminates mustard oil and causes epidemic dropsy. This toxin disrupts the oxidation of pyruvic acid, leading to its buildup in the blood. The accumulation of pyruvic acid results in the characteristic symptoms of epidemic dropsy, including acute swelling (edema) of the legs and other systemic complications. Thus, sanguinarine is the key harmful agent responsible for the development of epidemic dropsy following consumption of adulterated mustard oil.

Explanation for other options:

Clavine alkaloids (Option A): These compounds are linked to ergot poisoning, which leads to vasoconstriction and gangrene, but they do not cause dropsy.

BOAA (Option C): Found in Lathyrus sativus (grass pea), this toxin is responsible for lathyrism, characterized by spastic paralysis rather than edema or gastrointestinal issues.

Pyrrolizidine alkaloids (Option D): These alkaloids result in liver toxicity and veno-occlusive disease, but they are not associated with the sudden onset of dropsy symptoms.

question_text: What is most appropriate and effective means for prevention and control of CCHF:
option_a: Inactivated, mouse brain derived vaccine to animals and human
option_b: Tick control with acaricides in live stock farms
option_c: Personal protective measures in endemic areas
option_d: Chemoprophylaxis to persons with suspected exposure
explanation:
• Inactivated, mouse brain-derived vaccine to animals and humans: Incorrect. While research is ongoing, the inactivated, mouse-brain-derived vaccine is not widely available or considered the most effective control method.
  • Tick control with acaricides in livestock farms: Incorrect. Tick control can help reduce transmission in animals, but it does not comprehensively address human prevention, as CCHF also spreads via human-to-human contact and direct exposure to infected bodily fluids.
  • Personal protective measures in endemic areas: Correct. The most effective method for preventing CCHF is the use of personal protective equipment (PPE), such as gloves, masks, gowns, and eye protection, especially when handling livestock, patients, or deceased individuals in endemic regions.
  • Chemoprophylaxis to persons with suspected exposure: Incorrect. There is no established chemoprophylaxis for CCHF, and prevention primarily focuses on personal protective measures rather than medication.

Key Takeaways:

  • The most effective prevention for CCHF is the use of personal protective measures (PPE) in endemic areas.
  • Tick control and vaccines play a role in controlling animal-to-human transmission but do not address human-to-human spread directly.
  • Chemoprophylaxis is not a recommended preventive approach for CCHF.

Reference: NATIONAL HEALTH PROGRAMS OF INDIA, 12th Edition, J. Kishore, chapter-11, Page no.:412-416.

question_text: All are types of quarantine except-
explanation:
B. Relative Quarantine: Relative quarantine is not a recognized type of quarantine. It seems to be a term that is not commonly used in the context of public health measures. Therefore, option (B) is incorrect.

Explanation to why other options are not correct:

A. Absolute Quarantine: This type of quarantine involves strict isolation of individuals who are either confirmed or suspected to be infected with a contagious disease. It often entails physical barriers and restrictions on movement to prevent the spread of the disease. Absolute quarantine is typically enforced during severe outbreaks or pandemics when there is a high risk of transmission.

C. Modified Quarantine: Modified quarantine involves less stringent restrictions compared to absolute quarantine. It may include measures such as self-isolation at home, monitoring for symptoms, and limiting interactions with others. Modified quarantine is often implemented when the risk of transmission is lower or when individuals have been exposed to a contagious disease but are not showing symptoms.

D. Segregation: Segregation involves separating individuals who are infected with a contagious disease from those who are healthy. This can include isolating infected individuals in designated facilities or areas to prevent further spread of the disease. Segregation is commonly used in healthcare settings to prevent nosocomial infections and in communities during outbreaks to control transmission.

In summary, relative quarantine is not a recognized type of quarantine, making option (B) incorrect. Options (A), (C), and (D) describe different types of quarantine measures, with absolute, modified, and segregation being established concepts in public health practice.

Reference - Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 133

question_text: Which of the following statements about chickenpox (varicella) is correct?
option_a: Chickenpox is caused by the virus Herpes simplex
option_b: The varicella-zoster virus can remain dormant in the body and reactivate later in life, causing shingles
option_d: Chickenpox can only be transmitted through direct contact with the skin lesions
explanation:
• Chickenpox is caused by the virus Herpes simplex:
    • Not correct. Chickenpox is caused by the varicella-zoster virus, a member of the herpesvirus family, not Herpes simplex (which causes cold sores and genital herpes).
  • The varicella-zoster virus can remain dormant in the body and reactivate later in life, causing shingles:
    • After an initial chickenpox infection, the varicella-zoster virus can remain dormant in nerve tissue. It can reactivate later in life, typically due to a weakened immune system, leading to shingles, characterized by painful skin rashes.
  • Chickenpox primarily affects elderly individuals:
    • Not correct. Chickenpox primarily affects children, though adults who have never been infected or vaccinated can also contract it. Elderly individuals are more prone to complications from chickenpox, but not the primary group affected.
  • Chickenpox can only be transmitted through direct contact with the skin lesions:
    • Not correct. While direct contact with skin lesions is a mode of transmission, chickenpox is also spread through airborne droplets when an infected person coughs or sneezes.

Key Takeaways:

  • Varicella-zoster virus causes chickenpox and can later reactivate as shingles.
  • Chickenpox is primarily a childhood disease but can have complications in adults and the elderly.

question_text: A disease that displays vertical transmission is _____________________
explanation:
Vertical transmission refers to the transmission of a disease from a mother to her offspring during pregnancy, childbirth, or breastfeeding.

(A) Herpes: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) can be transmitted vertically from mother to baby during childbirth, especially if the mother has active genital herpes lesions at the time of delivery. The virus can be shed from the genital tract and infect the newborn during passage through the birth canal. This can result in neonatal herpes, which can cause severe complications or even death in newborns.

Explanation to why other options are not correct:

(B) Leprosy: Leprosy, also known as Hansen's disease, is primarily transmitted through prolonged close contact with untreated individuals who have leprosy. It is not typically transmitted vertically from mother to child during pregnancy or childbirth.

(C) Tetanus: Tetanus is caused by the bacterium Clostridium tetani, which is commonly found in soil, dust, and animal feces. Tetanus is acquired through the contamination of wounds or cuts with spores of the bacterium, rather than through vertical transmission from mother to child.

(D) Whooping cough: Whooping cough, or pertussis, is caused by the bacterium Bordetella pertussis. It is primarily transmitted through respiratory droplets from coughing or sneezing of infected individuals. It is not transmitted vertically from mother to child during pregnancy or childbirth.

In summary, herpes (option A) is the correct answer because it can be transmitted vertically from mother to baby during childbirth. The other options (B, C, and D) are not transmitted vertically and are transmitted through other means.

Reference - Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 105

question_text: A disease which is maintained in both humans and lower vertebrates can be transmitted in either direction is called ________
explanation:
(C) Amphixenosis:

Amphixenosis refers to diseases that are maintained in both humans and lower vertebrates and can be transmitted in either direction. In other words, these diseases can circulate between humans and animals, with transmission occurring from humans to animals and vice versa. This term accurately describes the scenario described in the question.

Explanation to why other options are not correct:

(A) Anthropozoonoses:

Anthropozoonoses refer to diseases that primarily infect animals but can be transmitted to humans. These diseases typically originate in animals and are transmitted to humans, but they do not necessarily involve transmission back to animals.

(B) Zooanthroponoses:

Zooanthroponoses are diseases that primarily infect humans but can be transmitted to animals. This term describes diseases where humans are the primary reservoir or source of infection, and they can spread to animals. It does not involve transmission from animals back to humans.

(D) Epornithic:

Epornithic refers to diseases that affect birds or are primarily associated with avian hosts. This term does not describe diseases that are maintained in both humans and lower vertebrates and can be transmitted bidirectionally.

In summary, option (C) Amphixenosis is the correct answer as it accurately describes diseases maintained in both humans and lower vertebrates that can be transmitted bidirectionally. It is distinct from the other options, which describe different types of disease transmission patterns.

Reference - Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 102

question_text: All are helpful in COVID 19 disinfection except
explanation:
(d) Use of mask: Wearing masks, particularly in indoor or crowded settings, is an essential preventive measure to reduce the spread of respiratory droplets containing the COVID-19 virus. Masks help protect both the wearer and others by reducing the transmission of respiratory droplets. Therefore, using masks is indeed helpful in preventing COVID-19 transmission, making this option incorrect in the context of the question.

Explanation to why other options are not correct:

(a) 70% ethanol: Ethanol, especially in concentrations of 70% or higher, is effective in disinfecting surfaces against the COVID-19 virus. It disrupts the virus's lipid membrane, leading to its inactivation. Therefore, using 70% ethanol for disinfection purposes is indeed helpful in combating COVID-19.

(b) 1% Glutaraldehyde: Glutaraldehyde is a chemical disinfectant commonly used in healthcare settings for high-level disinfection of medical equipment. It is effective against a wide range of microorganisms, including viruses like the one causing COVID-19. Therefore, 1% Glutaraldehyde can be helpful in disinfecting surfaces contaminated with the virus.

(c) Hand washing: Proper hand hygiene, including regular hand washing with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, is one of the most effective measures to prevent the spread of COVID-19. It helps remove viruses and other pathogens from the hands, reducing the risk of transmission. Hand washing is a crucial practice in maintaining personal hygiene and preventing the spread of infectious diseases like COVID-19.

In summary, all options except (d) are helpful in COVID-19 disinfection or prevention. Wearing masks is not a disinfection method but rather a preventive measure against the spread of the virus. Therefore, option (d) is the correct answer.
